books.section: Topic 6.11 Reform in the Gilded Age
Challenges to the Dominant Corporate Ethic
The Silver Issue and the Populist Movement

primary_sources: Thomas Nast, “The Brains,” Harper’s Weekly, October 21, 1871
Joseph Keppler, “The Bosses of the Senate,” Puck, January 23, 1889
Stereograph, “More Money! Less Misery! Good Roads!” Coxey’s Army approaching Washington, 1894, Library of Congress

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which farmers and workers challenged the power of corporations and political machines in the period 1865–1898.

documents.title: Nast on Boss Tweed
documents.source: Thomas Nast, “The Brains,” Harper’s Weekly, October 21, 1871. Public domain; image from the shared image pool.
documents.sourcing: A magazine cartoonist mocking the boss of New York’s Tammany Hall for readers across the country.

documents.title: George on Land and Labor
documents.source: Henry George, Progress and Poverty (1879), Book VII, Chapter 5. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A journalist and economist arguing that private property in land, not machines or population, caused poverty amid progress.
documents.text: “It is not that laborers have increased faster than capital; it is not that population is pressing against subsistence; it is not that machinery has made “work scarce;” it is not that there is any real antagonism between labor and capital—it is simply that land is becoming more valuable; that the terms on which labor can obtain access to the natural opportunities which alone enable it to produce, are becoming harder and harder.”

documents.title: The Bosses of the Senate
documents.source: Joseph Keppler, “The Bosses of the Senate,” Puck, January 23, 1889. Public domain; image from the shared image pool.
documents.sourcing: A satirical magazine cartoon drawn to show readers that trusts, not voters, ruled the Senate.

documents.title: The Hayseed Song
documents.source: “The Hayseed,” Farmers’ Alliance song, sung in Kansas in 1890. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A campaign song sung by Alliance farmers, turning their grievances into a call to vote.
documents.text:
“I was once a tool of oppression,
And as green as a sucker could be,
And monopolies banded together
To beat a poor hayseed like me.
The railroads and old party bosses
Together did sweetly agree;
And they thought there would be little trouble
In working a hayseed like me.
But now I’ve roused up a little
And their greed and corruption I see,
And the ticket we vote next November
Will be made of hayseeds like me.”

documents.title: The Sherman Act Outlaws Trusts
documents.source: Sherman Antitrust Act, Section 1, July 2, 1890. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A federal law written as the first national answer to combinations in restraint of trade.
documents.text: “Every contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, is hereby declared to be illegal.”

documents.title: The Omaha Platform on Government Power
documents.source: People’s Party, Omaha Platform, July 4, 1892, Preamble. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A new third party’s founding statement, written to rally farmers and workers behind a stronger government.
documents.text: “We believe that the power of government—in other words, of the people—should be expanded (as in the case of the postal service) as rapidly and as far as the good sense of an intelligent people and the teachings of experience shall justify, to the end that oppression, injustice, and poverty shall eventually cease in the land.”

documents.title: Coxey’s Army Approaching Washington
documents.source: Stereograph, “More Money! Less Misery! Good Roads!” Coxey’s Army approaching Washington, 1894, Library of Congress. Public domain; image from the shared image pool.
documents.sourcing: A commercial stereograph sold to the public, showing unemployed men marching toward Washington with banners demanding public-works jobs and an end to interest on bonds.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent of change or challenge, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as industrialization, urbanization, and the growth of corporations and cities in the Gilded Age.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Grange, the Knights of Labor, the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887, or the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document’s author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of change, showing that the same reform both challenged and left the old order standing, or explaining why one reform succeeded while another stalled.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Between 1865 and 1898 farmers and workers challenged corporate and machine power loudly and in new forms, building a press, a literature, a party, and a march on Washington, yet the challenge changed the argument more than the balance of power, since the trusts, the machines, and the courts largely held their ground.
Context: Railroads and corporations grew into national powers after the Civil War, while farmers faced falling prices and mortgages and workers faced long hours and low pay, and the two old parties offered neither group much help.
Evidence: Documents 1 and 3 show the press attacking machine and trust power, Nast’s money-headed Tweed and Keppler’s trusts towering over the Senate. Documents 2 and 4 show the ideas behind the challenge, George blaming land values and the Hayseed blaming monopolies and bosses.
Evidence continued: Documents 5 and 6 show the challenge reaching law and politics, the Sherman Act outlawing combinations and the Omaha Platform demanding a stronger government. Document 7 shows the challenge in the streets, Coxey’s unemployed marching on Washington.
Beyond the documents: The Grange organized farmers from 1867 and won Granger laws in the 1870s, the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 created a commission to regulate railroads, and William Jennings Bryan carried the free-silver cause in 1896.
Sourcing: Nast and Keppler drew for magazines that sold mockery, so their cartoons are arguments, not neutral reports; the Hayseed song is farmers speaking for themselves, while the Sherman Act is the law’s own words, showing how far Congress would go.
Complexity: The challenge was real and broad, yet it stalled where it mattered most, since the Sherman Act was soon read narrowly against unions, Bryan lost in 1896, and the Populist Party faded after its one strong election.
